references.text: When Lot and his family were led out of Sodom, they were told not to look back: "Do not look back" ([ref:1 Mos 19:17|Genesis 19:17]). Jesus uses Lot's wife as a warning against clinging to what one leaves behind.

Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt ([ref:1 Mos 19:26|Genesis 19:26]). This is the direct event Jesus refers to – she stands as a cautionary example of what happens when someone turns back to what they were meant to flee from.

In the immediate context, Jesus warns that whoever is on the roof must not go down to get their belongings ([ref:Luk 17:31|Luke 17:31]). Lot's wife illustrates the danger of hesitating and longing for what one has left behind.

Jesus expands on this principle further: "Whoever seeks to save their life will lose it" ([ref:Luk 17:33|Luke 17:33]). Lot's wife is an example of someone who tried to hold on to their old life and lost it.

Jesus said: "No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God" ([ref:Luk 9:62|Luke 9:62]). Looking back is a recurring theme in Luke – Lot's wife is the ultimate example.

The letter to the Hebrews urges believers not to draw back into destruction, but to have faith that leads to the salvation of their souls ([ref:Heb 10:38-39|Hebrews 10:38-39]). Lot's wife is an example of someone who drew back.

Paul describes forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead ([ref:Fil 3:13-14|Philippians 3:13-14]). This is the positive contrast to Lot's wife, who looked back instead of moving forward.
